> 「可以三十二相观如来不？」……「若以三十二相观如来者，转轮圣王即是如来。」……「若以色见我，以音声求我，是人行邪道，不能见如来。」

Section twenty-six is a trap set for the student who has learned the lesson too well.

Asked whether the Tathāgata can be contemplated by the thirty-two marks, 须菩提 — for the first time — says yes. Perhaps he means: after all, the marks are the tradition's own sign of a buddha.

The Buddha's reply is a single counterexample. If the thirty-two marks made someone a Tathāgata, then a wheel-turning king would be one. The wheel-turning king is the ideal worldly sovereign: righteous, immensely merited, and — by the old physiology of merit — in possession of the same thirty-two marks.

Same marks. Not a buddha. So the marks cannot be the criterion.

## Why 须菩提's yes matters

Throughout the sutra, 须菩提 has answered correctly. Here he answers wrongly, and the text keeps it.

The book reads this as deliberate: the failure is placed at this point because it is the failure of someone who has been following carefully. Having learned that marks are empty, one can still be caught by a *refined* mark — the marks of a buddha, which feel exempt because of what they signify.

The exemption is the error. Nothing is exempt.

## 转轮圣王 is not a straw man

The comparison is exact rather than rhetorical: the same marks, the same merit, a different attainment. The difference is not visible. Which is the point — no visible difference can certify an invisible one.

This has an immediate application. Every tradition has its version of the marks: credentials, lineages, robes, degrees, the unmistakable tone of someone who has arrived. Each of them can be earned without the thing.

## 若以色见我，以音声求我，是人行邪道

The section's verse is the most quoted passage in the sutra, and the most misapplied.

Whoever seeks me by form, or reaches for me by sound, is walking a wrong path and cannot see the Tathāgata.

The misapplication: therefore images are forbidden, chanting is forbidden, the senses are the enemy.

The book refuses this, and the refusal turns on one character. 邪道 here is not evil — not a demonic path, not a moral condemnation. It is a direction error: seeking in the wrong place, with the wrong expectation.

Bowing to an image to gather the mind is not this error. Bowing to an image in order to see a buddha is. Hearing a chant and letting it settle the body is not this error. Chasing a sacred sound because it seems to promise an encounter is.

## 法身 is not nothing

The section is about what the dharma-body is not, and the book adds one clause about what it is: 如 — suchness, the equal nature of all dharmas.

Not a void. Not an absence. Not a subtler body located somewhere else. The thing that cannot be seen by form or reached by sound is not hiding; it is the nature of what is already in front of you, which form and sound cannot deliver because they are what it is the nature of.

## The test

Name the marker by which you recognise spiritual authority. The tone, the vocabulary, the calm, the credentials, the following.

Then apply the counterexample: could someone possess all of it and not have the thing?

If the answer is yes — and it is always yes — then you have been using the marks, and the twenty-sixth section has just explained why that does not work.
